name: Neon Genesis Evangelion
blurb: Hideaki Anno's mecha anime about a lonely boy made to pilot a giant machine
aka: 新世紀エヴァンゲリオン
title: Neon Genesis Evangelion Explained: Story and Ending
description: Neon Genesis Evangelion explained: who is who, the TV story arc by arc, both endings (episodes 25–26 and The End of Evangelion) and the main themes.
h1: Neon Genesis Evangelion: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Neon Genesis Evangelion is a Japanese anime series created and directed by Hideaki Anno, made by Gainax with Tatsunoko Production and broadcast in 26 episodes from October 1995 to March 1996. Its story was finished again in the 1997 film The End of Evangelion. In 2015, fifteen years after a catastrophe called the Second Impact killed half of humanity, giant beings called Angels attack the city of Tokyo-3. Fourteen-year-old Shinji Ikari is summoned by the father who abandoned him and ordered to pilot Evangelion Unit-01, a giant humanoid machine, and the series uses the battles to explore the loneliness and fears of its characters.

body: Episodes 1–7. Shinji arrives in Tokyo-3 just as an Angel attacks. His father Gendo, whom he has barely seen in years, tells him to pilot Unit-01 or the badly injured Rei will have to. Shinji agrees and Unit-01 destroys the Angel when it goes out of control. He moves in with Misato, enrols at school, befriends Toji and Kensuke, and slowly forms a bond with Rei while fighting a new Angel every few episodes. The Evangelions are run by NERV, a secret agency under the United Nations, which answers in turn to SEELE, a shadowy committee.

Episodes 8–19. Asuka arrives from Germany with Unit-02 and moves in with Shinji and Misato. The three pilots learn to fight as a team. Unit-03 is taken over by an Angel while Toji is inside it; Gendo switches Unit-01 to an automatic Dummy Plug system, which tears Unit-03 apart and leaves Toji badly hurt while Shinji is forced to watch. Furious, Shinji quits, but returns when the Angel Zeruel overwhelms NERV, and Unit-01 goes berserk and devours the Angel. Shinji is then absorbed into the Eva for a month, where he relives memories of his mother Yui, who vanished in an experiment with Unit-01 years before.

Episodes 20–24. The series darkens. Kaji, who has been investigating NERV and SEELE, is killed. An Angel in orbit attacks Asuka's mind, forcing her to relive childhood trauma, and she falls into a breakdown. Rei sacrifices herself and Unit-00 to destroy another Angel, but a new Rei appears with no memory of Shinji. Ritsuko shows Misato and Shinji the truth: Rei is one of many clones, grown partly from Yui's remains, and Ritsuko destroys the spare bodies. Kaworu, sent by SEELE to replace Asuka, becomes the first person to tell Shinji he loves him, then reveals he is the final Angel and asks Shinji to kill him. Shinji does.
With the Angels gone, SEELE and Gendo each move to carry out the Human Instrumentality Project, a plan to dissolve the barriers between people and merge all human souls into one.

Episodes 25 and 26 (1996) take place almost entirely inside the characters' minds as Instrumentality begins. Using still frames, sketches, text cards and voice-over, they show Shinji, Asuka, Misato and Rei questioning why they exist and why they fear other people. Shinji realises that he can only value himself if he chooses to, and that the world can be other than how he sees it. In the final scene he stands in a circle of everyone he knows, who applaud and congratulate him, and he thanks them. The outside world and the fates of the characters are never shown.

The End of Evangelion (1997) retells episodes 25 and 26 from the outside. SEELE sends Japan's military to seize NERV. Misato is fatally shot getting Shinji to Unit-01, and Gendo kills Ritsuko. Asuka, discovering that her mother's soul is in Unit-02, wakes from her catatonia and destroys the troops, but is overwhelmed by the Mass Production Evangelions. Rei rejects Gendo, merges with the giant being Lilith, and Third Impact begins: every human dissolves into the primordial liquid LCL. Inside Instrumentality Shinji at first wants everyone gone, then rejects a world without other people, accepting that being with others means being hurt as well as loved. His mother Yui stays behind with Unit-01. Shinji wakes on a beach beside a red sea next to Asuka. He begins to strangle her, stops when she gently touches his face, and breaks down crying; Asuka says she feels disgusted. The film ends there.

Anno described the TV finale and the film as two alternative endings, like a game with multiple endings, rather than one replacing the other. Most viewers read the two as the same event, inner and outer: the TV episodes show Shinji's decision, the film shows its cost. Anno has said the series grew out of a long period of depression, and that he wanted the film to push fans to return from fiction to real life; many critics read Instrumentality as a picture of escapism. The beach scene itself is debated. Some see a hopeful, if painful, restart in which people can return if they choose to; others see Shinji and Asuka as unchanged and the ending as bleak.

ul: The hedgehog's dilemma: Misato and Ritsuko name the idea that people who get close inevitably hurt each other, which is the problem Instrumentality claims to solve.
Depression and self-worth: Shinji pilots to earn approval, and both endings turn on whether he can accept himself without it.
Parents and children: absent or damaging parents, Gendo, Yui and Asuka's mother, shape every young pilot.
Escape and reality: the series questions retreating into a comfortable dream, whether Instrumentality or fiction itself.
Religious imagery: Angels, Adam, Lilith and the Spear of Longinus borrow Christian and Kabbalistic names, used more as atmosphere than as doctrine.
Length: 26 TV episodes of about 24 minutes, plus The End of Evangelion (1997, about 87 minutes), which is best watched after episode 24.
Rebuild of Evangelion: four later films by Anno (2007, 2009, 2012 and 2021, ending with Evangelion 3.0+1.0 Thrice Upon a Time) retell the story and then diverge from it with a different ending.
Original: an original anime by Gainax; Yoshiyuki Sadamoto, the character designer, also drew a manga version (1994–2013).
Content advisory: violence and gore, psychological breakdown, suicidal thoughts and sexual content, especially in The End of Evangelion.

check.why: Ritsuko shows that Rei is one of many clone bodies, made partly from Yui's remains.

check.q: Where does The End of Evangelion finish?
options: On a beach beside a red sea
check.why: Shinji wakes after Third Impact on a beach next to Asuka, and the film ends there.

faq.q: Should I watch The End of Evangelion after episode 26?
faq.a: The usual order is episodes 1–24, then The End of Evangelion, then episodes 25 and 26 if you want to see the inner version. Watching all 26 episodes first and then the film also works; the film covers the same time as the last two episodes.

It is the secret plan of SEELE and Gendo to remove the barriers between individuals and merge all of humanity into a single being, ending loneliness and conflict. SEELE wants it as an evolution of the species; Gendo wants it to be reunited with his dead wife Yui.

faq.q: Are the Rebuild films the same story as the series?
faq.a: The first film closely follows the opening episodes, but the later films change characters, events and the setting, and the last one gives the story a different conclusion.
